title: See why 3x + 5 = 20 gives x = 5
learningGoal: Choose inverse operations by reading the structure of an equation, while preserving equality.
teachingApproach: Treat equality as balance, connect each visible change to notation, contrast a one-sided change, and generalize the undoing strategy.

clips.title: Read before calculating
clips.bigIdea: The equation describes three equal unknown groups with five extra units.

segments.narration: Before calculating, notice that three equal x groups and five extra units balance a total of twenty.

clips.title: Equality must survive every move
clips.bigIdea: An operation is valid only when it preserves the equal value of both sides.

segments.narration: The equals sign is a promise that both sides have the same value, so every move must preserve that promise.
Removing five units from each pan is the picture; subtracting five from both sides is the matching algebra.

clips.title: Undo in reverse order
clips.bigIdea: Remove the outer added quantity before separating the equal x groups.

segments.narration: Five was added after the three groups were formed, so undo that outer addition first on both sides.
The balance now says three equal x groups share fifteen units.
Splitting fifteen equally across three groups gives five in each group, so x equals five.

clips.title: A tempting move breaks equality
clips.bigIdea: Changing only one side produces a different, false equation.

segments.narration: Subtracting five only on the right changes the promise; subtracting five on both sides preserves the same equation.

clips.title: The reusable pattern
clips.bigIdea: Solving isolates the unknown by undoing operations in reverse order.

segments.narration: The reusable strategy is not subtract then divide blindly; it is undo the operations surrounding x in reverse order.

clips.title: Check it, then recognize it
clips.bigIdea: Substitution verifies this answer, while structure reveals the same method in a new equation.

segments.narration: Putting five into the original expression gives twenty, so the value satisfies the equation we started with.
In four x plus three equals nineteen, the numbers change but the same clue says to undo the added three first.

interactions.prompt: Why must the same operation be applied to both sides?

options.label: Only to make the work shorter

interactions.correctFeedback: Correct. Matching operations preserve the equality represented by the equation.
interactions.incorrectFeedback: Think about the two balanced pans: changing one pan alone destroys the equality.

transferCheck.prompt: What should you undo first, and why?

options.label: Subtract 3 from both sides because +3 is the outer operation
Divide only the left side by 4 because x has coefficient 4

transferCheck.correctFeedback: Yes. Read the structure and undo the outer addition while preserving equality.
transferCheck.incorrectFeedback: Follow the operations around x backward, and preserve equality on both sides.

completion.title: You saw the idea behind the operations.
completion.body: The method is to read the equation's structure, preserve equality, undo operations in reverse, and verify in the original.
